chapter_theme: After the discus kills the king of the Vidyadharas, the enemy dead are burned and their wives withdraw, the defeated bow and are shown mercy, the hero meets his father and is bathed and crowned Vasudeva, and the seven royal jewels come to him.

cast.role: the red-eyed tall one, hero who takes the discus and is crowned Vasudeva
the elder prince, brother of Tivittan
the father of the two princes, named here as lord of the land of Surama
the Vidyadharas, who give up their pride and bow
the Vidyadhara and allied kings who crown and bathe the hero
the brahmins who lay the dead king on his pyre
the weeping women whose tears fall in 1482
the queens of the dead Vidyadhara king, called here Vayakkiriva

1482.reading: The weeping of the women flows like streams, and with it the great king's wrath, likened to the fire at the world's end, is put out.
1482.nuance: The first two lines are about the women and kings who weep, the last two about the anger that goes out; who exactly the kings melting are, and whose anger is meant, is not fixed by the words, so the reading keeps to the image of tears as water on fire.
1482.event: The tears of the grieving women quench the victor's long-burning anger.

1483.reading: The brahmins lay the king of the mountain folk on a bed of cotton, silk and fine cloth, after he has been brought down from his elephant, and put him into the bright fire.
1483.nuance: The dead king is called one of untainted fame (line 4), so the funeral is given with honour to the enemy slain; the verse does not name him, and he is taken from the context to be the lord of the mountain Vidyadharas.
1483.event: Brahmins lay the dead Vidyadhara king on a rich bed and give him to the funeral fire.

1484.reading: The kinsmen, sons and kings who fell in the battle are given to the fire on the field, and the king's defeated men leave weeping.
1484.nuance: Line 4 is broken in the word division and the relation of 'those who could not complete what they thought' to the king is a guess.
1484.event: The attendants of the beaten king burn the fallen on the battlefield and depart in tears.

1485.reading: The queens of the dead Vidyadhara king strip off their ornaments, go to the Vidyadhara world, and bar desire's way with the fence of chastity and the lock of restraint, shutting the doors of the senses.
1485.nuance: Chastity is shown as a fence the widows themselves build around the senses, not as a guard set on them by others; whether this is a turn to renunciation or only widowhood is not said.
1485.event: The widowed queens put off their jewels and shut out desire.

claims.claim: a woman's chastity and self-restraint fence off desire, and the senses are doors that can be locked

1486.reading: A rain of flowers falls on the head of the red-eyed hero who has won the shining discus, and mingles with the sound of drums and conches.
1486.event: Flowers are showered on the discus-winner as drums and conches sound.

1487.reading: The divine arrows he shot are cut down and he takes the shining discus, and the sky is filled with a cry that it is a great marvel.
1487.nuance: The subject is not named in the verse; 'the hero who took the discus' is taken from 1486 and 1499.
1487.event: The hero cuts down the divine arrows and takes the discus, and the sky resounds with wonder.

1488.reading: The Vidyadharas lay down their fierce anger and pride, and bow to the hero, the colour of a dark jewel-mountain, saying they were greatly afraid.
1488.event: The Vidyadharas give up their pride and bow to the victor in fear.

1489.reading: The hero shows mercy to the frightened kings and has a drum sounded for the kin of the king who died there, bidding them live again in the Vidyadhara world.
1489.nuance: The speech is reported, not quoted, so the speaker is given as the hero from the action of line 4.
1489.event: Tivittan has a drum proclaim that the dead king's people may return and live.

claims.claim: a conquering king should grant mercy and let the defeated kin live

1490.reading: The dark-cloud-coloured hero alights from Garuda, mounts a rumbling elephant, and enters the camp amid the kings' praise.
1490.event: Tivittan comes down from Garuda and rides to the camp as kings praise him.

1491.reading: Radiant like the moon, he goes with the great elder brother to the father's holy feet and bows, wearing a shoulder garland of gold.
1491.nuance: 'The great one' is taken to be the elder brother Vijayan; the verse does not give the name.
1491.event: Tivittan and his elder brother go to their father and bow at his feet.

1492.reading: The king of the land of Surama, his eyes wide with delight at his sons' might, speaks to the kings who stand beside and bow.
1492.event: The father, pleased with his sons' prowess, addresses the kings who bow around him.

1493.reading: He says that he reached the name of father of these flawless young princes through his penance, and asks to see in their royal state the beloved jewel-adorned eyes of his sons.
1493.nuance: The father credits his own tapas, not his sons' worth, for the blessing; this is the same turn of phrase as Kural 70's question of what penance the father did.
1493.event: The father says his fatherhood is the fruit of penance and asks to see his sons crowned.

claims.claim: being the father of fine sons is the fruit of penance

1494.reading: At his word the Vidyadhara king and the kings joined with him gladly crown the princes, and the royal drum sounds that day.
1494.event: The Vidyadhara king and the kings crown the princes to the beat of the royal drum.

1495.reading: The kings bathe him in the waters of the Ganga and Sindhu, poured from golden lotus-mouthed pots in the auspicious way.
1495.event: The kings pour Ganga and Sindhu water on him from golden pots.

1496.reading: They pour on the king's curled head waters of the milk sea, taken up by the divine host and carried in pots of shining gems, so it is said.
1496.nuance: Who the bearers are is carried by the verb alone; 'the divine army' (line 1) is taken as the source of the water.
1496.event: Divine hosts pour milk-sea water from gem pots on the king's head.

1497.reading: The brave Vidyadhara kings bathe the one like Indra with the flowers and waterfalls of the Mandara jewel-mountain and bow to him, as the tale says.
1497.event: The Vidyadhara kings bathe him in waters of Mandara and bow.

1498.reading: Lakshmi comes with love, and by the form, the light and the old rule of the book the king is anointed protector of the world.
1498.nuance: The third and fourth lines turn on a rare phrase for the book's rule; the sense that the anointing follows a scripture's rule is held loosely.
1498.event: The dark-cloud one is anointed protector of the world, with Lakshmi drawn to him.

1499.reading: Because he took the discus after killing the discus-king, they set on him a bright crown and name him Vasudeva.
1499.nuance: The title is given by the fact of winning the discus (line 2, 'because it was the discus'), not by birth or an earlier anointing.
1499.event: The kings crown the discus-winner as Vasudeva.

claims.claim: the discus won in battle is the sign of the title Vasudeva

1500.reading: They crown the great hero in the old manner with a long crown of the gods, and bless him as the protector whose feet ring with anklets.
1500.event: The kings and gods crown the great hero in the ancient way and bless him.

1501.reading: At the great festival of the royal coronation they honour the gods, and the other precious things unsent also reach him.
1501.nuance: Line 2 and 4 are not fully clear about whether the treasures come from the gods or from the festival.
1501.event: The coronation festival is held and the remaining treasures come to the king.

1502.reading: He wins the discus, staff, sword, conch, bow, parasol and fire-jewel, and shines as the god the kings of men bow to.
1502.event: The king receives the seven royal jewels and shines as a god before kings.

claims.claim: the possessor of the discus and the other royal jewels is a god among kings of men

1503.reading: The two great treasures named Valampuri and the golden lotus pour out gems, bright gold and shining gold ore.

1504.reading: Crowned with a blazing crown, with all kings worshipping at his feet, the lord reaches the great hall of the discus's wealth.
1504.event: The crowned lord enters the great hall of the discus's riches as kings worship.

1505.reading: The great divine jewels each go to the city made ready, and the palace is held in honour because of the unwearying Garuda and the shining lord.
1505.nuance: Lines 3-4 name Garuda and the lord together but the syntax is ambiguous about who is honoured by whom.
1505.event: The divine treasures go to their prepared city and the royal palace is honoured.

links.note: 1482 has the women's tears put out the victor's wrath like water on fire; Kural 555 says the tears of the afflicted wear away a king's wealth.
links.teaches: Tears are a force against a king in both, but the epic turns them to a mercy that ends the fire while the Kural makes them a loss that grows.

gains.a: The scene gains a rule: the victor is shown ruled by the weeping, as the couplet says a king should dread.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case where the tears act at once and quench, not only wear away over time.

links.note: 1483 lays a king on a bed of silk and gives him to the fire; Naladiyar 21 says kings under moon-like umbrellas have been carried off and called dead.
links.teaches: The fire takes the proud king as the quatrain says it takes all, and the honour of his funeral does not alter that.

gains.a: The funeral gains the quatrain's lesson that rank is no shelter from death.
gains.b: The quatrain gains a named king whose cotton and silk bed does not save him.

links.note: 1485 shows the queens barring desire with the fence of chastity and the lock on the senses; Kural 57 calls a woman's own restraint the best guard.
links.teaches: The epic's widows guard themselves by their own restraint, which is the kind the Kural prefers to confinement.

gains.a: The widows' act gains a test: it is the self-made guard the couplet praises.
gains.b: The couplet gains a case at the point of greatest loss, after the husband's death, where outside guard has gone.

links.note: 1488 has the beaten Vidyadharas bow in fear; 1489 has the victor answer with mercy and a drum for the dead king's kin.
links.teaches: The fear of the defeated is answered with grace, which turns a conquest into a settlement.

links.note: 1493 has the father say he reached fatherhood through penance; Kural 70 says the son's help to the father is the question of what penance he did.
links.teaches: The father in the epic asks the question the couplet puts in others' mouths, so the son's worth is credited back to the father's penance.

gains.a: The father's remark gains a rule that a worthy son is the world's proof of his father's penance.
gains.b: The couplet gains a father who answers it himself, making the saying his own humble claim.

links.note: 1499 crowns the hero because the discus won the war; Kural 546 says victory comes from the sceptre that does not bend, not from the spear.
links.teaches: The epic gives the title to the winner of the weapon, which the Kural would call a lesser ground than justice.

gains.a: The crowning gains a stricter standard: is the discus a better ground than a straight sceptre?
gains.b: The couplet gains a king whose title rests on the weapon, which tests its claim that the spear gives no victory.

source_issues: Verses 1482-1485 were printed as eight half-lines and joined into four lines by the build.
Verse 1484 line 4 is broken in word division.
Verse 1500 line 1 had a stray pulli removed by the build.
